q: You use useEffect with a dependency but it runs more than expected. The dependency is an object created inline. Why?
options: Objects are not valid useEffect dependencies
A new object is created on every render so React sees it as always changed
useEffect only works with primitive dependencies
You need to JSON.stringify the object first
explain: Objects are compared by reference not value. An inline object literal creates a new reference on every render so useEffect thinks the dependency changed every time. Memoize it with useMemo.

q: You wrap a child in React.memo but it still re-renders when the parent renders. The parent passes a function as a prop. Why?
options: React.memo does not work with function props
A new function reference is created on every parent render breaking memo's shallow comparison
The child needs to be wrapped in useCallback too
React.memo only prevents re-renders caused by state changes
explain: React.memo uses shallow prop comparison. A function created inline gets a new reference every render so memo sees it as a changed prop. Wrap the function in useCallback to stabilize the reference.

q: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
options: useMemo is for components, useCallback is for hooks
useMemo memoizes a computed value, useCallback memoizes a function reference
They are identical — useCallback is just shorthand for useMemo
useCallback runs after render, useMemo runs before
explain: useMemo caches the result of an expensive computation. useCallback caches the function itself. useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps).

q: Your Context value changes frequently and causes all consumers to re-render even when they don't use the changed part. What is the fix?
options: Use useReducer instead of useState in the provider
Split the context into separate contexts by concern
Wrap all consumers in React.memo
Move the context provider closer to the consuming components
explain: Every consumer re-renders when any part of the context value changes. Splitting into separate contexts means components only re-render when the specific context they consume changes.

q: You use useReducer instead of useState. When is useReducer the better choice?
options: When you need to persist state to localStorage
When state logic is complex with multiple sub-values or actions
When you have more than 3 useState hooks in a component
When state needs to be shared across components
explain: useReducer is better when state updates involve multiple values that change together or when next state depends on complex logic. It centralizes update logic making it easier to test and reason about.

q: You have an expensive calculation in a component that runs on every render. How do you fix it?
options: Move the calculation outside the component
Wrap the calculation in useMemo with the relevant dependencies
Use useEffect to run the calculation after render
Use useCallback to cache the calculation function
explain: useMemo caches the result of a calculation and only recomputes when its dependencies change. useCallback would cache the function not the result.

q: What is reconciliation in React?
options: The process of syncing state between parent and child components
React's algorithm for comparing the old and new virtual DOM to find minimal DOM updates
The process of merging context values from multiple providers
React's way of handling errors in the component tree
explain: Reconciliation is React's diffing algorithm. It compares the previous virtual DOM with the new one and computes the minimum number of real DOM operations needed to update the UI.

q: You change a key prop on a component. What does React do?
options: Updates only the changed props on the existing component instance
Completely unmounts the old component and mounts a fresh one
Triggers a forced re-render without resetting state
Nothing — key only affects list rendering
explain: Changing a key tells React this is a different element. It destroys the old component instance including all its state and creates a fresh one. This is a useful trick to reset a component.

q: You read a state value inside a useEffect but always get the initial value even after updates. What is wrong?
options: State values cannot be read inside effects
The state variable is missing from the dependency array causing a stale closure
You need to use useRef to read state inside effects
useEffect always runs with the initial render values
explain: When a state variable is not in the dependency array the effect closes over its initial value and never updates. Adding it to the array ensures the effect always uses the latest value.

q: What is a custom hook and when should you create one?
options: A hook that overrides built-in React hooks
A function starting with use that extracts reusable stateful logic from components
A hook that only works inside class components
A performance optimization that replaces useState
explain: Custom hooks let you extract and reuse stateful logic across multiple components. They must start with use and can call other hooks. They are the main way to share logic in modern React.

q: You call useState with an expensive initial value computation. It runs on every render. How do you fix it?
options: Move the computation outside the component
Pass a function to useState instead of the value directly
Use useMemo to wrap the useState call
Use useRef to store the initial value
explain: Passing a function to useState as lazy initialization means React only calls it on the first render. Passing the value directly executes the computation every render even though it's only used once.

q: You need to render a component outside its parent DOM hierarchy like a modal. What do you use?
options: React.Fragment
React.createPortal
useRef with document.body.appendChild
React.lazy with Suspense
explain: createPortal renders children into a different DOM node than the parent component. The component still lives in the React tree so context and events work normally.

q: What is an error boundary in React?
options: A try/catch block inside a React component
A class component that catches JavaScript errors in its child tree and shows a fallback UI
A hook that prevents components from throwing errors
A React context that propagates errors up the tree
explain: Error boundaries are class components that implement componentDidCatch or getDerivedStateFromError. They catch rendering errors in their subtree and display a fallback instead of crashing the whole app.

q: You batch multiple state updates in React 18. How does this differ from React 17?
options: React 18 removed batching entirely
React 18 automatically batches all updates including those in setTimeout and promises, React 17 only batched event handlers
React 17 batched more updates than React 18
Batching in React 18 requires opt-in with a special API
explain: React 17 only batched state updates inside React event handlers. React 18 introduced automatic batching everywhere — setTimeout, promises, native events — reducing unnecessary re-renders.

q: Your component re-renders too often and you suspect an inline object in JSX is the cause. How do you verify?
options: Add console.log to every prop
Use React DevTools Profiler to see what triggered the render
Wrap every prop in useMemo
Move all objects to a database
explain: React DevTools Profiler shows exactly which components rendered, how long they took, and what caused them to render. It is the right first step before optimizing.

q: You need to forward a ref from a parent to a child component's DOM element. What do you use?
options: Pass ref as a regular prop
React.forwardRef to wrap the child component
useImperativeHandle in the parent
Attach the ref directly to the child component tag
explain: Refs are not regular props — they cannot be passed directly. React.forwardRef creates a component that receives the ref as a second argument and can attach it to an inner DOM element.

q: What is useImperativeHandle used for?
options: To access the parent component's methods from a child
To customize what a parent sees when it accesses a child's ref
To imperatively trigger re-renders without state
To replace useEffect for imperative side effects
explain: useImperativeHandle lets a child component expose a custom API through its ref instead of the raw DOM node. Useful when a parent needs to call specific methods on a child.

q: You see a warning about each child in a list needing a unique key. You use the array index as the key. Why is this problematic?
options: Index keys are not valid in React
When items reorder or are removed the index shifts causing React to map state to the wrong element
Index keys cause infinite re-render loops
Array indices are too large for React to process
explain: Index as key breaks when items are reordered or removed. React maps the key to a component instance so shifting indices cause state from one item to bleed into another.

q: What is the purpose of the dependency array in useCallback?
options: It lists the arguments the callback accepts
It tells React when to create a new function reference
It prevents the callback from running more than once
It defines which components can call the function
explain: useCallback returns the same function reference as long as dependencies haven't changed. When a dependency changes React creates a new function. This prevents unnecessary re-renders in memoized children.

q: You want to show a loading spinner while a lazy loaded component loads. What wraps it?
options: React.memo with a loading prop
Suspense with a fallback prop
ErrorBoundary with a loading state
useEffect that sets isLoading to false when done
explain: Suspense catches the loading state thrown by React.lazy and renders the fallback UI until the component bundle is ready.

q: What is the problem with defining a component inside another component's render?
options: It causes a syntax error
React creates a new component type on every render causing the inner component to always remount
Inner components cannot access the outer component's props
It only works with class components
explain: Defining a component inside render creates a new component type reference every render. React sees it as a completely different component and unmounts then remounts it losing all state.

q: You need to trigger an animation after a state update but the DOM hasn't updated yet when you read it. What hook fixes this?
options: useEffect — it always runs after DOM updates
useLayoutEffect — it runs synchronously after DOM mutations before paint
useMemo — it precomputes values before render
useRef — it gives direct DOM access
explain: useLayoutEffect fires synchronously after React updates the DOM but before the browser paints. This is the right place to read layout or trigger animations that depend on DOM measurements.

q: What happens when you return a function from useEffect?
options: It becomes the new effect for the next render
React calls it as cleanup before the next effect runs and on unmount
It prevents the effect from running again
It is called with the previous dependency values
explain: The function returned from useEffect is the cleanup function. React runs it before the effect re-runs on dependency change and when the component unmounts.

q: You have deeply nested state and updating it requires spreading every level. What is the recommended solution?
options: Use a global variable for deep state
Use Immer to write mutating-style updates that produce immutable state
Flatten all state to avoid nesting
Use useRef for nested state to avoid immutability rules
explain: Immer lets you write state updates as if you're mutating directly but produces immutable results. Redux Toolkit uses Immer internally. It eliminates deep spread chains.

q: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components in forms?
options: Controlled components use refs, uncontrolled components use state
Controlled components have their value driven by React state, uncontrolled components manage their own DOM state
Uncontrolled components cannot be validated
There is no practical difference in React 18
explain: Controlled components store form values in React state making React the source of truth. Uncontrolled components let the DOM manage the value accessed via ref only when needed.
